name: Eyelid sebaceous gland carcinoma
aliases: sebaceous gland carcinoma of the eyelid

reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / WHO Classification of Eye Tumours
clinicalPearls: An aggressive periocular malignancy arising chiefly from the meibomian glands of the tarsus and the glands of Zeis, favouring the upper eyelid
It is the great masquerader of the eyelid, mimicking a recurrent chalazion or chronic unilateral blepharoconjunctivitis and thereby delaying diagnosis
A firm, yellowish, or recurrent eyelid nodule, loss of eyelashes (madarosis), and destruction of the meibomian gland orifices should raise suspicion
Pagetoid spread of malignant cells through the conjunctival and eyelid epithelium produces diffuse, clinically deceptive involvement and complicates margin control
Histology shows lobules of atypical cells with foamy lipid-laden cytoplasm; lipid stains on fresh tissue and markers such as adipophilin and EMA support the diagnosis
Management is complete excision, often Mohs micrographic surgery or wide excision, with map (conjunctival) biopsies to map pagetoid spread and radiotherapy in selected cases
An association with Muir-Torre syndrome links the tumour to mismatch-repair deficiency and internal malignancy, warranting consideration of hereditary cancer screening
reference.pathophysiology: Eyelid sebaceous gland carcinoma is a malignant tumour of sebaceous differentiation arising predominantly from the meibomian glands within the tarsal plate and the glands of Zeis at the lid margin, with the upper eyelid most often affected. Malignant cells proliferate as lobules and sheets with atypical nuclei and characteristic finely vacuolated cytoplasm reflecting intracytoplasmic lipid. A defining behaviour is pagetoid intraepithelial spread, in which individual malignant cells migrate through the overlying conjunctival and epidermal epithelium, producing diffuse periocular involvement that mimics inflammatory disease and obscures the true tumour extent. A subset occurs within Muir-Torre syndrome, where germline mismatch-repair deficiency predisposes to both the sebaceous neoplasia and associated visceral cancers. The tumour spreads to regional preauricular and cervical nodes and can invade the orbit.
additionalDifferentials: Basal cell carcinoma of the eyelid
Squamous cell carcinoma of the eyelid or ocular surface squamous neoplasia
Ocular cicatricial pemphigoid (for chronic conjunctival inflammation)
additionalInvestigations: Full-thickness eyelid biopsy of any suspicious or recurrent lesion
Lipid staining on fresh (frozen) tissue and immunohistochemistry including adipophilin and EMA
Map (multiple conjunctival) biopsies to delineate pagetoid intraepithelial spread
Mismatch-repair protein immunohistochemistry and consideration of Muir-Torre evaluation
Regional lymph node assessment (preauricular and cervical) and orbital imaging for staging
Ophthalmic examination to assess conjunctival and orbital involvement
redFlags: A recurrent chalazion that fails to resolve or recurs after drainage
Chronic unilateral blepharoconjunctivitis unresponsive to conventional treatment
Madarosis or destruction of eyelid margin architecture over a firm lesion
Diffuse conjunctival injection suggesting pagetoid spread or orbital signs suggesting invasion
Personal or family history pointing to Muir-Torre syndrome
reference.prognosis: Eyelid sebaceous carcinoma is aggressive, and prognosis worsens with delayed diagnosis, larger tumours, extensive pagetoid spread, and orbital or nodal involvement; complete excision of localised disease gives a reasonable outlook, but regional or distant spread carries significant mortality.
pitfalls: Treating a recurrent eyelid lesion repeatedly as a chalazion without biopsy and delaying diagnosis
Underestimating margins because of occult pagetoid intraepithelial spread
Failing to test for mismatch-repair deficiency and missing an underlying Muir-Torre syndrome
Overlooking orbital or nodal involvement during staging
